scenes.text: Start with the front panel. IceCube has sixty-four O S F P connectors. So how can the switch offer a hundred and twenty-eight eight-hundred-gigabit Ethernet interfaces?

Follow one transmit signal. It starts at the switch A sick, beneath the cold plate on the Switch Main Board. The signal travels electrically over high-speed flyover cables to a Physical Interface Card. At the faceplate, the pluggable module converts the electrical signal to light and sends it out through fiber.

Zoom in on one connector. With Meta's dual eight-hundred-gigabit module, one connector carries two independent eight-hundred-gigabit Ethernet interfaces. Each of the two interface cards carries thirty-two connectors. Multiply sixty-four by two by eight hundred gigabits per second. That's one hundred and two point four terabits per second.

The specification also lists five hundred and twelve two-hundred-gigabit Ethernet interfaces. That's the same total capacity at a different interface rate. When reading a port count, ask whether it describes the faceplate or the configured interfaces.

IceCube slides into a two Open Unit space in an Open Rack version three High Power Rack. A canister adapter fits the switch to the rack. Here, the rack supplies power and connects the switch to the coolant loop.

Inside, liquid-cooled cold plates carry heat away from the switch A sick and the O S F P optics. Follow the other path from the front of the switch to its rear fans. That airflow cools the microserver, the baseboard management controller, the power stages, the solid-state drive, and the Q S F P twenty-eight management module.

Now look directly at the rear. Coolant enters on your right through a blind-mate coupling. It returns on your left. The central connector mates to the rack's D C power busbar. Between the coolant couplings, four fans draw air through the chassis.
Back at the front, two optical form factors sit near each other. Which uses liquid cooling? The O S F P bank uses cold plates. The Q S F P twenty-eight depends on airflow.
Look at the rear of IceCube. There are four fan trays. Suppose one fan drops below its expected speed while the switch is running. How does the platform find out?

Programmable logic measures fan speed in revolutions per minute. If the reading is too low, the logic reports a warning to the microserver through a register. The microserver also uses temperature readings to calculate a fan speed command. The warning and the command travel in opposite directions.

IceCube splits platform management between the microserver and the baseboard management controller, or B M C. The microserver handles sensor readings and the fan-speed algorithm. The B M C handles power-on, failure recovery, and system event logging.
The rear fan trays are replaceable in the field, and the front gives access to the E one dot S solid-state drive. Before you move on, name the controller that runs the fan-speed algorithm.
